title: Wanting the best school for your kid doesn't make you a hypocrite https://www.salon.com/2026/09/23/wanting-the-best-school-for-your-kid-doesnt-make-you-a-hypocrite/
author: Alex Galbraith
summary: Alex Galbraith treats Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay as a piece that tore through liberal corners of the internet by exposing the gap between educational idealism and the hyper-competitive reality of American schooling. He reads her account as a heartbreaking portrait of a systemic problem, underfunded schools with burnt-out staff, that no single family could reverse. The debate that followed, he says, collapsed into whether wanting the best for one's child betrays egalitarian ideals. Galbraith answers no: society should fund good schools for all children, but in the meantime parents get only one shot at raising their kids. He draws on his own Florida public schooling and his coming child in all-charter New Orleans, and he compares the fight to familiar charges of hypocrisy aimed at progressives who benefit from their own wealth.
points: Galbraith frames the Hannah-Jones controversy as an example of a reliably viral genre about the welfare of children.
He reads the essay as showing a systemic problem that one engaged family could not fix from within.
The core question, whether choosing the best school for your child makes a liberal a hypocrite, gets a firm no.
He notes that in all-charter New Orleans the scramble for good schools is built into a lottery system, removing the neighborhood choice altogether.
He links the dispute to recurring accusations that progressives must personally sacrifice to prove their policy beliefs.
quotes: Over the weekend, one such piece tore through the well-meaning liberal corners of the internet — meaning Bluesky and Threads, mostly — and prodded at the gap between educational idealism and the hyper-competitive reality of schooling in America.

Overworked and burnt-out staff teaching the children of overworked and burnt-out adults isn’t a recipe for educational success, and Hannah-Jones’ recollection of her repeated frustrations and conversations with educators paints a heartbreaking picture of a systemic issue that no one family could reverse.

In the end, Hannah-Jones’ daughter succeeded against the odds, landing in a great test-in school. But it’s hard to come away from her story believing that such a result would be attainable for others.
Once the column hit the web, it quickly devolved into a fight over whether wanting the best for your child is a betrayal of egalitarian ideals.
We should have well-funded schools for all American children, where success isn’t so tied to where you call home and the relative affluence of your neighbors.

Hannah-Jones’ experiment might be novel, but the fight that broke out around it is familiar. You can see it anytime an outwardly progressive politician or commentator benefits from their personal wealth.
